step_text: Deploy a marine survey team to conduct a detailed visual and sonar survey of the vessel’s hull-to-ground contact points, assessing structural integrity, potential hull breaches, and the extent of grounding damage. Document all visible damage and take measurements for future calculations.

Establish a secure salvage perimeter using buoys and warning flares to prevent unauthorized access and ensure safety of personnel and nearby vessels. Coordinate with local authorities and maritime traffic control to restrict navigation in the area.

Deploy heavy-duty winches and anchor chains from a tugboat or barge positioned offshore to apply controlled tension on the vessel’s bow and stern, gradually lifting it off the beach. Use multiple points of attachment to distribute force evenly and prevent further hull damage.

Install temporary watertight bulkheads or inflatable barriers around the vessel’s waterline to prevent seawater ingress during the lifting operation, especially if any minor leaks are detected. Monitor bilge levels and prepare pumps for immediate response.

Coordinate with a marine crane or floating crane vessel to provide additional lifting power if the tugboat’s winches are insufficient. Position the crane to lift the vessel’s stern or bow, depending on the angle of grounding, and use hydraulic jacks to stabilize the vessel during the lift.

Once the vessel is fully afloat, conduct a stability assessment and prepare for towing to a safe harbor or dry dock. Secure all loose equipment, ensure all crew are accounted for, and prepare the vessel for inspection and repair before final salvage operations.

Deploy a multi-vehicle underwater inspection team (ROV and divers) to assess the extent of hull breaches, internal flooding, and structural integrity, while mapping the wreck’s orientation and identifying potential access points for intervention.

Establish a fire suppression team with foam and high-pressure water cannons to extinguish visible flames and smoldering areas, prioritizing the engine room and ammunition compartments to prevent secondary explosions or fire spread.
Deploy a heavy-lift barge or crane vessel to position a temporary buoyancy platform near the starboard side of the wreck to stabilize the listing hull and prevent further sinking or capsizing.

Install temporary watertight bulkheads or inflatable barriers around the most breached sections to contain flooding and prevent water ingress into critical compartments, using materials available on board or from nearby vessels.

Coordinate with marine engineers to pump out water from accessible compartments using portable pumps and deploy a temporary drainage system to reduce the vessel’s weight and improve salvageability, while monitoring for hazardous materials or fuel leaks.

Prepare for controlled refloating by attaching heavy-duty mooring lines and winches to the wreck’s remaining structural points, then use tugs to slowly and carefully pull the vessel upright or to a stable position, while continuously monitoring for structural failure or further fire outbreaks.

Deploy a survey team with sonar and depth-finding equipment to map the grounding location, determine the extent of hull contact, and assess seabed composition to avoid further damage during operations.
Establish a safety perimeter using buoys and VHF radio alerts to prevent additional vessels from entering the hazard zone and to coordinate with local maritime authorities.
Deploy heavy-duty winches and anchor chains from a tugboat or barge to secure the vessel and apply controlled tension to the hull, preventing further sinking or structural collapse.
Install temporary pontoons or flotation devices around the vessel’s submerged sections to reduce the load on the hull and stabilize the vessel’s position.
Use hydraulic jacks or shore-based cranes to lift the vessel’s stern or bow, depending on the list, to reposition it to a more stable orientation for refloating.

Once stabilized, initiate a controlled refloat operation using tugs and ballast pumps to remove water from the vessel’s compartments and gradually raise it to a safe draft, then guide it to a secure anchorage or dry dock for permanent repairs.

Immediately establish a secure perimeter around the vessel using marine traffic control and local law enforcement to evacuate all civilians from the beach and promenade, ensuring public safety and preventing unauthorized access to the hazardous area.

Deploy fire-fighting assets including fireboats, foam cannons, and aerial firefighting units to suppress the fire from multiple angles, prioritizing the containment of flames to prevent spread to adjacent structures or cargo. Coordinate with naval fire control teams for precise targeting.

Conduct a rapid damage assessment using remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and divers to evaluate the extent of structural damage, identify potential fuel or hazardous material leaks, and determine if the vessel is structurally stable enough to be refloated or if it is beyond salvage.

Deploy salvage barges and heavy lifting equipment to position the vessel for stabilization. If the vessel is still partially afloat, use winches and anchors to secure it and prevent further drifting or sinking. If the vessel is in danger of sinking, prepare for emergency ballast operations or use of buoyancy aids.

Coordinate with naval engineering and salvage teams to develop a refloating or towing plan. This may involve pumping out water, installing temporary supports, or using tugboats to maneuver the vessel to a safe location for further assessment or disposal.

Prepare for potential environmental remediation by deploying oil spill response teams and containment booms if fuel or hazardous materials are confirmed to be leaking. Monitor the situation continuously and update the salvage plan as new information becomes available.

Conduct a preliminary site assessment to determine the exact grounding location, depth of submersion, and type of seabed (sand, mud, rock, etc.) using sonar or divers. Evaluate weather and sea state conditions to determine if salvage operations can proceed safely, and monitor the vessel’s position for any movement due to tides or currents. (Applies: AGRROUND - Conditions at scene, weather, position observation, seabed type)

Deploy divers to inspect the vessel’s hull for structural integrity, leaks, and damage to the keel or bilge areas. Check for any trapped personnel and assess if the vessel is stable enough to be moved. (Applies: AGRROUND - Condition of vessel, stability, crew safety; CAPSIZED - People aboard, vessel condition)

Secure the vessel to prevent further movement by deploying fenders, mooring lines, or temporary anchors to stabilize it against wave action and tidal currents. (Applies: AGRROUND - Position observation, local conditions)

Mobilize tugboats and heavy-lift barges to the scene. Use tugs to apply controlled force to pull the vessel free, while barges can be used to support the vessel’s weight or provide counterbalance. Ensure equipment is suitable for the vessel’s size and weight. (Applies: AGRROUND - Equipment suitability, larger vessel complexity)

If the vessel is partially submerged, deploy pumps to remove water from the hold to reduce weight and improve buoyancy. If the vessel is heavily damaged, prepare patching materials to seal any leaks before attempting to move it. (Applies: AGRROUND - Cargo load relevance, vessel condition; SUNKEN - Water management, hull inspection)

Coordinate with local authorities and environmental teams to monitor for any fuel or cargo leaks and deploy booms or absorbents if necessary. Once the vessel is free, plan for its safe towing to a dry dock or repair facility, ensuring all hazardous materials are secured and documented. (Applies: SUNKEN - Fuel/cargo management, environmental hazards; RESOURCES - Booms, pumps, cranes, tugs)

Deploy fireboats and firefighting support vessels to establish a perimeter around the wreck and commence firefighting operations. Prioritize extinguishing the visible fire using foam or water mist systems to prevent escalation and reduce risk of explosion from fuel or ammunition. Ensure all firefighting equipment is inspected and operational before deployment (ON FIRE assertion).

Conduct a preliminary hazard assessment of the wreck site, including checking for potential oil, fuel, or chemical spills that may have been released from ruptured tanks or cargo holds. Deploy booms and absorbent materials to contain any surface pollution and prevent environmental contamination (SUNKEN assertion).

Deploy divers to inspect the wreck’s condition, focusing on the extent of hull breaches, flooding levels, and structural integrity. Divers must be briefed on the risks of entering the vessel and must avoid actions that could destabilize the wreck or cause further damage (SUNKEN assertion; CAPSIZED assertion). Document findings for engineering planning.

Establish a salvage command center on a nearby support vessel to coordinate operations. Assemble the response crew (divers, engineers, firefighters, rescue personnel) and identify available resources such as tugs, cranes, pumps, and patching materials. Assess the depth of the wreck and determine if it is within the operational range of available lifting or recovery equipment (SUNKEN assertion; RESOURCES assertion).

Begin controlled flooding or ballasting operations if the vessel is deemed stable enough to be stabilized for potential lifting or refloating. If the vessel is too deep or structurally compromised, consider deploying a heavy-lift barge or crane to remove critical components or stabilize the wreck to prevent further sinking or collapse (SUNKEN assertion; AGROUND assertion).

Monitor the wreck’s position and condition continuously throughout the operation. Adjust tactics based on weather, sea state, and visibility. If the vessel is deemed beyond economic or safe recovery, prepare for controlled demolition or abandonment procedures in accordance with environmental and safety protocols (AGROUND assertion; SUNKEN assertion).

Deploy a survey team including divers and engineers to assess the vessel’s position, the type of ground it is resting on (e.g., sand, mud, rock), and the extent of hull damage or structural integrity. This step is critical to determine the feasibility and method of refloating, as per the assertion that “the type of ground the vessel is resting on may affect how difficult it is to move” and “the condition of the vessel may affect what options are available to responders.”

Conduct a safety and environmental assessment of the area around the vessel to identify potential hazards such as submerged obstructions, hazardous cargo (if any), or fuel leaks. This aligns with the assertion that “the area around the sunken vessel may need to be checked for potential hazards before work begins,” even though the vessel is aground, and “fuel or cargo aboard the vessel may need to be considered before the hull is interfered with.”

Coordinate with local maritime authorities and deploy appropriate resources including tugboats, barges, and pumps. Tugboats should be selected based on their power and suitability for the vessel’s size and weight, as per the assertion that “equipment used to move the vessel may need to be suitable for its size and weight.” Pumps may be used to remove water from the vessel’s compartments to reduce weight and improve buoyancy.

Establish a secure perimeter around the vessel using buoys and warning signals to prevent further accidents and to keep other vessels at a safe distance. This is important to manage “local conditions such as currents and visibility” and to ensure “the position of the vessel may need to be kept under observation throughout the operation.”

Implement a refloating plan using tugs to apply controlled force to the vessel’s bow or stern, depending on the grounding point. The plan should include a gradual and monitored approach to avoid sudden movements that could cause further damage or destabilize the vessel, as per the assertion that “care may be needed throughout the operation to avoid causing further damage to the vessel.”

Once the vessel is refloated, conduct a post-salvage inspection to assess any damage to the hull, machinery, or cargo. This step ensures that any necessary repairs or further actions are planned, and it aligns with the assertion that “the condition of the vessel may affect what options are available to responders.” The vessel should then be secured and towed to a safe location for further assessment and repair.

Immediately deploy fireboats and firefighting support vessels to the scene to establish a perimeter and begin applying foam or water suppressants to the fire source. Ensure all firefighting equipment is checked and operational before deployment. Coordinate with local authorities to evacuate any people on or near the vessel if possible, and ensure the safety of onlookers on shore by cordoning off the area with barriers or directing them away from the smoke plume.

Conduct a rapid visual and drone-assisted assessment of the vessel’s condition, focusing on the location and intensity of the fire, potential fuel sources (e.g., oil tanks, ammunition, cargo), and structural integrity of the hull. Divers or engineers should be prepared to inspect for breaches or flooding if the fire is extinguished or if the vessel begins to list. This assessment will guide subsequent actions and determine if the vessel is salvageable or requires abandonment.

Deploy tugs and support barges to position themselves around the vessel to stabilize it and prevent it from drifting into hazardous areas or colliding with shore infrastructure. Monitor the vessel’s position continuously, as weather and sea state may change, and adjust the positioning of tugs accordingly. Ensure that the vessel’s movement is controlled to avoid exacerbating the fire or causing further damage.

If the fire is contained or extinguished, initiate a hull inspection to assess damage and determine if the vessel can be refloated or towed to a safe location for repair. If the vessel is deemed beyond repair, prepare for abandonment and ensure that any hazardous materials (fuel, cargo, etc.) are secured or contained using booms and pumps to prevent environmental contamination. Coordinate with environmental and maritime authorities for spill response.

If the vessel is deemed salvageable, develop a detailed salvage plan that includes the use of cranes, pumps, and patching materials to remove water, repair structural damage, and prepare the vessel for towing. Ensure that all equipment is suitable for the vessel’s size and weight. Monitor weather and sea conditions to determine the optimal time for salvage operations, as adverse conditions may limit the time available for work.

Once the vessel is stabilized or the fire is under control, conduct a final inspection to ensure that all hazards have been mitigated and that the vessel is safe for any further operations. If the vessel is to be towed, coordinate with tugboats to execute the towing plan, ensuring that the vessel is moved to a safe location for repair or disposal. Document all actions taken and report to the relevant authorities for record-keeping and future reference.

Deploy a dedicated tide gauge and continuous monitoring station at the grounding site to track the vessel’s reaction to the rising tide. This will determine if the vessel can refloat naturally on the next high tide without active intervention. If the tide is insufficient, proceed to step 2.

Conduct a comprehensive survey of the vessel’s fuel and cargo holds by the dive and survey team. Verify that all fuel tanks are empty or have residual fuel quantified and secured, and that all cargo holds are inventoried and assessed for hazardous materials. This is critical before any cutting, welding, or movement begins (Assertion: All fuel tanks must be checked...; All cargo holds must be checked...).

If the vessel is a large vessel (>50 m), initiate lightering operations using barges to remove weight from the vessel’s superstructure or cargo holds, ensuring weight is removed from areas other than the neutral loading point to reduce ground reaction (Assertion: Larger vessels require lightering...; Weight removal must avoid the neutral loading point...).

If the vessel is a deep-draft vessel (>10 m draft), deploy ocean-going salvage tugs and/or beach gear/anchor-wire-chain systems to provide the necessary pulling force. Calculate the required pulling force based on the ground reaction and seabed friction coefficient (Assertion: Deeper-draft vessels require tug assistance...; The required pulling force depends on the ground reaction...).

If the grounding is on hard substrate (rock or coral), deploy a dredging operation to clear a channel around the vessel before any pulling attempt (Assertion: Hard grounding on rock or coral requires dredging...).

Once the vessel is deemed ready for refloat, execute a controlled refloat using the appropriate towing equipment (harbor tugs or ocean-going salvage tugs) while continuously monitoring the vessel’s stability and ground reaction. After refloat, conduct a post-refloat assessment for structural damage and flooding (Assertion: All fuel tanks must be checked...; Post-righting, the hull and internal spaces must be reassessed...).

Deploy a dive and survey team to conduct a thorough underwater assessment of the hull integrity, internal flooding, and cargo status. Before any entry, the team must perform three sequential gas tests (explosive gas, oxygen, toxic gas) in each compartment they plan to enter. This is required by assertion SUNKEN-1 to ensure safety before any hull disturbance or hot work begins.

Confirm the vessel’s position and depth using side-scan sonar or electro-acoustic sonar to map the wreck and locate any submerged oil or hazardous materials. This is critical to assess environmental risk and plan recovery, especially if the vessel is in a sensitive habitat (assertion SUNKEN-7). The survey must also identify the extent of structural damage and the location of any remaining fuel or cargo.

Initiate fuel offloading from all accessible tanks using submersible pumps or remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) before any hull disturbance. This is mandated by assertion SUNKEN-3 to prevent uncontrolled spillage during salvage operations. The salvage team must inventory and account for all cargo before any disturbance, as unknown cargo may include hazardous materials requiring specialist handling (assertion SUNKEN-4).

Deploy a floating crane or barge-based lifting system to begin controlled sectional removal of the vessel’s main body. Given the side-lying position, the crane must be positioned to lift sections without causing further structural collapse. The lifting loads must be kept within rated limits and controlled continuously to avoid overturning (assertion CAPSIZED-7). A salvage engineer or naval architect must verify the lift plan (assertion CAPSIZED-8).

Deploy containment booms and skimmers around the wreck to manage any surface oil spill. If submerged oil is detected, use electro-acoustic sonar to locate it and deploy diver or ROV recovery systems. This is required to match the oil’s behavior and prevent environmental contamination (assertion SUNKEN-6).

After the vessel is stabilized and all hazardous materials are secured, conduct a final stability assessment to determine if the vessel can be refloated or towed. If refloating is feasible, use ocean-going salvage tugs and beach gear to apply controlled pulling force, calculating the required force based on ground reaction and seabed friction coefficient (assertion AGROUND-7). If refloating is not feasible, the vessel should be declared a total loss and prepared for final disposal under environmental regulations.

Deploy a dedicated tide gauge at the grounding location to monitor the tidal rise and calculate the ground reaction force. This will determine if the vessel can refloat naturally on the next high tide without active intervention.

Conduct a preliminary survey using a dive and survey team to assess the nature of the grounding surface (e.g., sand, mud, rock) and check for any structural damage to the hull. This will inform the required pulling force calculation based on seabed friction coefficient.

Check all fuel tanks and cargo holds for residual fuel and hazardous materials before any movement or cutting begins, as per the assertions. This is critical to prevent uncontrolled spills during any refloat or lightering operations.

If the vessel is larger than 50 meters (which appears to be the case based on its size and structure), initiate lightering operations to reduce displacement. This must be done by removing weight from areas other than the neutral loading point to ensure a reduction in ground reaction.

If the grounding is on a hard substrate (rock or coral), arrange for dredging to clear a channel before any pulling attempt. If the substrate is soft (mud or sand), proceed to pulling using beach gear or anchor-wire-chain systems, with tugs providing assistance if the draft exceeds 10 meters.

Calculate the required pulling force based on the ground reaction and seabed friction coefficient. Deploy ocean-going or harbor tugs as appropriate, and execute the pulling operation under the supervision of a salvage engineer or naval architect to ensure the force is controlled and within safe limits. Monitor the vessel’s response throughout the operation.

Immediately evacuate all personnel from the vicinity of the vessel, including the beach crowd and any cyclists, to ensure no one is exposed to potential fire spread, toxic fumes, or explosion risk. Establish a safe perimeter at least 50 meters from the vessel’s hull.

Deploy fireboats with external monitors to provide boundary cooling to the vessel’s fire-affected areas and adjacent compartments, preventing fire spread and reducing the risk of backdraft. Do not direct monitors into the fire space itself.

Activate the vessel’s fixed CO₂ or foam suppression system only after confirming the space is clear of all personnel. If the vessel has a CO₂ system, ensure the pre-discharge alarm sounds before gas release. If foam is available, confirm it is alcohol-resistant (AR) foam if the vessel carries water-soluble or polar-solvent cargo.

Deploy a dive and survey team to assess the hull integrity, internal flooding, and cargo status. Before any entry, conduct three gas tests in sequence: explosive gas, oxygen, then toxic gas. This is critical before any cutting, welding, or movement begins.

If the vessel is carrying hazardous materials or unknown cargo, deploy hazmat or ordnance specialists to secure and inventory the cargo before any hull disturbance. Offload fuel from all tanks before any salvage work begins to prevent uncontrolled spill.

Once the fire is confirmed out and the vessel is stable, reassess its stability and structural integrity. If the vessel is still afloat and seaworthy, deploy harbor tugs for controlled towing to a safe anchorage. If the vessel is damaged beyond repair, prepare for sectional removal using floating cranes and barges.
